newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa's Manuel to walk budget tightrope.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Manuel to walk budget tightrope.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel has little scope for surprises in his maiden budget on Wednesday if he is to meet his goal of cutting the deficit to four percent of GDP, analysts said.
But edgy financial markets could take heart from a sharply- reduced borrowing requirement and a move to ease foreign exchange controls.
"It's another year of walking the fiscal tightrope," Dave Mohr, chief economist at life assurer Old Mutual, told a pre-budget briefing on Tuesday.
"Government is facing severe spending demands but has committed itself to very severe budget disciplines in term of GEAR (the Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy)."

With a rise in Value Added Tax (VAT) ruled out on political grounds, no big tax changes are seen -- apart from increases for tobacco, alcohol and fuel, and moves to stop inflation eroding tax revenues.

Manuel's repeated pledge to meet his GEAR goal of a deficit before borrowing of four percent of gross domestic product in 1997/98, down from 5.1 percent this year, means there is rare consensus among economists over the big budget numbers.

Mohr said he was looking for a nominal nine percent increase in spending to 192 billion rand ($43.4 billion) with revenue up 13 percent at 166.5 billion. That compares with a Reuter consensus poll of analysts of around 190 billion and 165 billion respectively.

Improved tax collection will be a central part of the programme while on the spending side the government will have to get tough on the public sector wage bill, which accounts for 37 percent of total outlays, to achieve a real spending cut.

But Manuel still has a card up his sleeve in the form of privatisation proceeds, after announcing he would not use cash from the sale of state assets or strategic oil stocks to meet the deficit target. This leaves open the possibility that some of the money will be used to cut actual borrowing.

With a deficit of around 25 billion and redemptions in 1996/97 (April-March) of some 10 billion, South Africa would face a gross borrowing requirement of some 35 billion rand, against a revised 39 billion rand this year.

But this could be reduced by up to five billion rand using privatisation receipts while a further three billion is likely to come from foreign bond issues and two billion through Treasury bills, according to Sanlam economist Jac Laubscher.

That would leave 25 billion to be raised in local bonds, or 15 billion in new money if loans redeemed are rolled over, against 21.9 billion in 1996/97 -- a figure Laubscher said would be "extremely positive" for the bond market.

Privatisation proceeds, notably from the sale of 30 percent of telecommunication utility Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium and a further 10 percent to local black interests, may also embolden Manuel on exchange control relaxation, by lifting reserves.

But analysts are divided as to whether the budget is the right place for details on the next moves on easing capital controls -- expected this time to focus on individuals -- or whether there will merely be a declaration of intent.
The next steps in the gradual phasing out of controls are expected to be modest, but psychologically important.
The markets are demanding action on an issue which is seen as a major impediment to investor confidence, by artificially locking unwilling capital in South African assets.
"If there is no announcement on exchange controls that will be a major disappointment for the markets," said Mohr.
